opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's a great question, and honestly it's one of the less flashy but really practical areas where I think LLMs shine. A lot of real-world data work isn't building fancy models. It's the messy part before that: you have customer records in one system, invoices in another, maybe some spreadsheets someone maintained by hand, and they don't line up. Names are spelled differently, addresses are formatted differently, one source says "IBM" and another says "International Business Machines Corp."

Traditionally, you'd handle that with rule-based matching, fuzzy string matching, maybe some hand-engineered features and a classifier for entity resolution. That works, but it's brittle. You keep adding rules for edge cases. LLMs are good here because they bring a lot of world knowledge and a sense of semantic similarity. They know that "Bob" and "Robert" are probably the same person, or that two product descriptions worded completely differently refer to the same item.

Schema mapping is another area. If you have two tables with columns like "cust_dob" and "date_of_birth," or more ambiguous cases, an LLM can propose mappings pretty reliably. That used to be a lot of tedious manual work.

That said, I'd be careful about using them as the sole decision-maker. I like a hybrid setup: use cheap, deterministic methods first to narrow down candidate matches, then use the LLM on the ambiguous cases, ideally having it output structured results and maybe a short justification you can audit. And keep a human in the loop for high-stakes merges. You don't want an LLM confidently merging two different patients' medical records, for example.

There's also the cost and scale side. If you have millions of records, you can't just throw every pair at a large model. But you can use a smaller fine-tuned model, or use embeddings for blocking and retrieval and only call the bigger model where it adds value. So for me it's less "LLMs replace the data pipeline" and more "LLMs handle the fuzzy, judgment-heavy part that used to require a person squinting at two rows in a spreadsheet."

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, that's a good question, and it's actually one of the use cases I find most practical. So, I think where LLMs really shine is in the messy, unstructured parts of data reconciliation, the stuff where traditional rule-based approaches break down because you'd need an endless list of edge cases.

A classic example is entity matching. You have a customer record in one database that says "IBM Corp." and another that says "International Business Machines," and a third that has a typo in it. Historically you'd write fuzzy matching rules, maybe some string distance metrics, and you'd still get a lot of false positives and false negatives. An LLM, because it has this world knowledge baked in, can look at those and say, these are probably the same entity. And it can do that with addresses, product names, job titles, all these fields where the semantics matter more than the exact characters.

Another area is schema mapping. If you're merging data from two systems and one has a column called "cust_dob" and the other has "birth_date," a human can see those are the same, but automating that used to be painful. LLMs are quite good at proposing those mappings, and then you can have a human verify them rather than build them from scratch.

That said, I'd add a caveat, which is that I wouldn't use an LLM as the final arbiter. I see it more as a candidate generator or a first-pass tool. You let the model propose matches or mappings, maybe with some confidence estimate, and then you have validation logic or a human in the loop for the ambiguous cases. Because the model can be confidently wrong, and in data reconciliation, a silent error can propagate through everything downstream.

And for a lot of these tasks, you honestly don't need the largest model. A smaller model, or even a fine-tuned one on your specific domain, can be more cost-effective and sometimes more reliable, because it's a fairly constrained task. So I'd say the sweet spot is combining the LLM's flexibility for the fuzzy semantic parts with deterministic checks for the parts where you actually know the rules.

astra-6.text:
I think one useful application is when you have information in different formats and there isn’t a clean way to join it. Say one source is a database, another is a collection of PDFs, and another is notes written by people. They might all describe the same thing, but use different names or different levels of detail. An LLM can help extract the relevant information and map it into a common structure.

The tricky part is distinguishing between two sources saying the same thing differently and two sources actually disagreeing. If they disagree, you don’t necessarily want the model to pick whichever answer sounds more plausible. You want it to surface that discrepancy and preserve where each piece of information came from.

So I see it as particularly useful for getting messy, unstructured information into a form where you can compare it, apply rules, and have a person review the ambiguous cases.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they’re especially useful when the sources don’t quite speak the same language. You might have a customer database, support tickets, and product documentation, and each uses slightly different names or descriptions for the same thing. An LLM can help map those concepts together, where a strict keyword match or a set of rules might miss the connection.

The interesting part is handling that ambiguity. Are these two records referring to the same entity? Does this description correspond to that field in another system? The model can propose a mapping, and then you can use more conventional checks—or a human reviewer—to verify it. I’d be more cautious about asking it to decide which source is correct when they conflict. Recognizing that two pieces of information are related is different from knowing which one is authoritative.
